articles.title: What Does a Museum Need? Inside the Exhibition Architecture of the Natural History Museum Oslo
articles.description: Designing a museum interior means negotiating between the needs of the collection and those of the visitor: objects must be protected and carefully displayed, while spaces need to remain accessible, legible, and engaging. Scale, circulation, security, lighting, structure, and technology all become part of the design, often working quietly in the background so that the exhibits remain the focus. So, how do you fit 4.5 billion years of Earth's history into a museum interior? The renovation of the Natural History Museum Oslo , home to one of the largest geological and anthropological exhibitions in the Nordic countries, offers a clear example of how these demands can come together within an existing architectural framework.

articles.title: House of Wall Forest / IGArchitects
articles.description: This house was designed for a couple and their child on a uniquely shaped site resembling a crab's claw, with a greenway to the south and a transmission tower standing to the east. Rather than imposing a single, unified order onto the site conditions or the surrounding urban environment, the design began by incorporating multiple orientations that respond directly to the site itself. Through a cluster of wall-columns rising at different angles, the walls are conceived to act collectively—as a group—embedding shifts in direction and distance within the space and creating a buffer-like territory between urban conditions and everyday life.

articles.title: Labor-management conflicts in Telco are spreading
articles.description: As telecom companies expand the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in areas previously handled by existing staff, such as customer service and quality control, labor-management conflicts are emerging over the AI adoption process and job security. The labor union argues that, since AI will affect employment and performance evaluations, labor and management must reach an agreement before its implementation. On the other hand, management counters that if the agreement process before AI implementation is expanded, management decisions could be delayed. There are concerns that similar conflicts are likely to recur because there is no clear standard for determining whether the adoption of AI falls under a company’s management rights or whether it is subject to collective bargaining. A cellphone store in downtown Seoul on April 9. / News1 According to industry sources on the 2nd, the LG Uplus Minju Uplus union recently demanded that the company conduct a prior labor-management agreement regarding the introduction of AI. The union stated, “We demand job security so that the introduction of AI does not lead to job insecurity,” adding, “We raised concerns about potential problems that may arise during job retraining and evaluation processes related to AI use.” The New Union, KT’s second-largest union, is also demanding that worker protection in the course of the AI transition be included in the bargaining proposal. The reason telecom labor unions have raised specific concerns about AI adoption is that AI is rapidly penetrating even tasks that were previously handled by humans. Its application scope is expanding beyond AI Customer Service Centers (AICC) to include network monitoring, marketing, activation, and quality management. LG Uplus is using AI for consultation quality management and agent training. In the past, because quality managers could not evaluate all consultations, which averaged 1.5 million per month, only selected and inspected a portion of them. After introducing “AI Auto QA,” a large language model (LLM)-based agent coaching solution, LG Uplus is now using AI to review all consultation content. After analyzing the consultation content, AI directly informs the counselor of areas for improvement. For example, if a representative says, “You have a 5G pricing plan,” they are told that the correct expression is, “You have a 5G pricing plan.” KT CS, which operates KT Customer Service, announced that as of June 2026, its AI voice bot automatically handles about 30% of all incoming calls, totaling 1.5 million calls per month. It goes beyond AI assisting agents with their tasks by handling the calls that agents used to answer themselves. In its Q1 2026 earnings announcement, KT stated that it would enhance operational efficiency by introducing AI throughout the entire process, from consultation and sales to activation and post-sales customer satisfaction (CS) management. It means expanding the scope of AI application from customer center support and training to sales, activation, and customer service operations. This year, SK Telecom assigned employee numbers, affiliation, job roles, and authority to its AI agents. SK Telecom defined AI not merely as a simple work-assist tool, but as a new agent of work that works together with its members. A union official at a telecommunications company said, “As AI is rapidly transforming the work of the telecommunications industry, there needs to be a mechanism to protect workers’ rights.” On the other hand, a telecom official responded, "While the union can raise concerns about the introduction of AI as an issue, there has never been any artificial workforce reduction due to AI adoption," adding, "Customer service is a job category with a high turnover rate, so it is difficult to directly link workforce changes to AI adoption." Some in the industry point out that requiring prior agreement with labor unions every time AI is introduced is unrealistic given the pace of technological advancement. An anonymous official said, "Generative AI, which has only recently emerged, has already become part of everyday life, showing how rapidly it is advancing. In a rapidly changing industrial environment, every time AI is introduced, if prior agreement is reached with labor unions, companies may fall behind in competition with others." The civic group pointed out that job insecurity caused by the introduction of AI is already a foreseeable problem. As AI use continues to spread, similar conflicts may recur, so there is a call for the government to establish clear standards between protecting workers and companies’ use of AI. Han Seok-hyun, head of the Citizen Mediation Office at Seoul YMCA, said, “While the government and industry focused on accelerating the pace of AI development, they have relatively neglected workers’ job insecurity caused by AI adoption.” He added, “Government ministries must clearly establish standards for companies’ AI adoption and use so that they can protect workers.” fun3503@chosunbiz.com

articles.title: UN adopts Pakistan-led resolution on access to assistive technology
articles.description: WASHINGTON: The UN General Assembly on Wednesday adopted by consensus a Pakistan-led resolution aimed at improving global access to affordable assistive technology, particularly in developing countries. The resolution, titled ‘Access to Assistive Technology’, is the first-ever General Assembly resolution specifically devoted to the issue. Introducing the resolution, Pakistan’s permanent representative to the UN, Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad, said around 2.5 billion people worldwide needed one or more assistive products, devices or related services, but millions continued to face barriers to accessing them. “These barriers included high costs, limited availability, inadequate infrastructure and services, restricted access to technology and shortages of trained personnel,” he added. Assistive technology includes a wide range of products and services, from wheelchairs, prosthetic limbs and hearing aids to screen readers, communication devices and other digital solutions. Such technologies can help children attend school, enable adults to work, allow older people to maintain independence and facilitate the fuller participation of persons with disabilities and certain health conditions in society. “These are not simply products or devices,” Mr Ahmad said, describing assistive technology as “the bridge between dependence and independence; between exclusion and participation; between potential and opportunity”. The resolution links access to assistive technology with wider development and inclusion objectives, including education, employment, healthcare, social protection and participation in society. The resolution places particular emphasis on developing countries, calling for greater international cooperation, financing and technical assistance for countries facing resource and capacity constraints. It also recognises that the need for assistive technology does not disappear during emergencies. Countries are encouraged to incorporate such technology into humanitarian preparedness and response, including during armed conflicts and natural disasters. The resolution was drafted and negotiated by Counsellor Saima Saleem, Pakistan’s first visually impaired career diplomat and a user of assistive technology. Her involvement, the Pakistani mission said, brought a direct personal perspective to an initiative focused on how technology could enhance independence, opportunity and equal participation. Pakistan has previously played a leading role in advancing the issue at the international level. In 2018, it initiated World Health Assembly Resolution 71.8 on improving access to assistive technology, which was also adopted by consensus. Published in Dawn, September 3rd, 2026
